solutions.check: bars rebuilt from the blog's numbered answers (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Classics, to him, may be represented by such philosophical method

indicators.note: to be represented anew is to be presented again in a different form, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: all thirteen letters of these three words are used

explanation.surface: A thinker sees the classics through the lens of a particular philosophical approach.
explanation.walkthrough: SCHOLASTICISM is the medieval schoolmen's method, built on classical authors such as Aristotle, so the classics really were represented by it.
explanation.definitionFit: Scholasticism is the logical, disputational method of medieval philosophy, so it is exactly a philosophical method of this kind.

clue.text: Second oldster in Gretna Green landmark?

parts.note: S is the standard abbreviation for second
in naval slang an oldster was a midshipman of four years' standing, and a middy is a midshipman

explanation.surface: An elderly person is the second famous sight at Gretna Green.
explanation.walkthrough: Oldster is not a pensioner but old naval slang for a senior midshipman. Gretna Green is the Scottish border village where runaway couples married in the blacksmith's shop.
explanation.definitionFit: Smiddy is the Scots word for a smithy, and the Gretna Green blacksmith's shop is the village's famous wedding venue; the question mark flags the example.

clue.text: Artery cuts turn out red

indicators.note: something that cuts into a thing goes into its middle, splitting it in two

parts.note: to come out as, to turn out
the M1 is Britain's main motorway artery, written MI

explanation.surface: Severed arteries make the blood come out red.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is about blood, but the artery is a road: the M1 motorway from London to Leeds, read as the letters MI.
explanation.definitionFit: Red is slang for a communist, and commie is the informal, dismissive word for the same person.

clue.text: Plant fruit and veg on top of stone — odd

parts.note: a hip is the fruit of the rose
a pea is a vegetable
st is the abbreviation for the stone weight
rum is British slang for odd or strange

explanation.surface: A gardener sets fruit and veg on a stone and finds the effect strange.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'on top of' simply stacks the first pieces above the stone.
explanation.definitionFit: Hippeastrum is a genus of bulbous flowering plants, the ones commonly sold as amaryllis.

clue.text: Office lot going wild in old dance

indicators.note: something going wild runs out of control, so the letters lose their order

parts.note: office is an old euphemism for a lavatory, shortened to lav
the three letters rearranged

explanation.surface: The whole office lets its hair down at a period-themed dance.
explanation.definitionFit: Lavolt, also lavolta or volta, was a lively leaping dance for couples popular in Elizabethan times.

clue.text: Disappointed parishioner may find this accommodation with shared facilities (11, two words)

definitions.meaning: first meaning, read as a phrase: a church service that falls flat
second meaning: a rented flat with cleaning and other services provided

explanation.walkthrough: The first half is cryptic: the churchgoer's dull Sunday service was flat. The second half is the straight meaning of the compound noun.
explanation.definitionFit: A service flat is a rented apartment whose rent includes domestic services such as cleaning, sometimes with shared amenities.

clue.text: Profits turn out fine, as of old

definitions.note: plural, where issue is a collective noun in this legal sense
definitions.meaning: first meaning: in law, the ... of land are its profits or produce
second meaning: to result or emerge
third meaning: fine in its old sense of end or conclusion, as in 'in fine'

explanation.walkthrough: Three meanings run together. 'Fine' is not the penalty but the archaic word for an end, which an issue (outcome) also is.
explanation.definitionFit: Issue covers produce or proceeds from property, the verb to emerge or result, and an outcome or ending.

clue.text: Questioner on the spot disheartened the conceited, first off

indicators.note: with its first removed, the word drops its opening letter

parts.note: in place, present: in

indicators.note: losing heart means losing the middle, so only the outside letters of the word survive

parts.note: the word keeps only its outside letters
the conceited are arrogant

explanation.surface: An interrogator on the spot deflates the vain, picking them off first.
explanation.definitionFit: An interrogant is an old word for one who asks questions, an interrogator.

clue.text: Such Capone always retained — 'capo di tutti …'

definitions.text: Such Capone always retained — 'capo di tutti …'

parts.note: surface reading: some kind of Capone, the Chicago gangster boss
setter's reading: the thing Capone's nickname named, a mark he kept on his face for life; 'capo' is Italian for head

explanation.surface: A mafia boss of bosses always held on to his kind of thing.
explanation.walkthrough: Capone was nicknamed Scarface after the knife wound on his cheek; 'capo di tutti capi' (boss of all bosses) nods at his head and face.
explanation.definitionFit: A scar is a permanent mark left on the skin by a healed wound, like the one on Capone's cheek.

clue.text: The writer penning dig nastily — one may generate gall

indicators.note: acting nastily means behaving badly, so the letters are put in disorder
to pen something is to shut it in, like animals in a fold

parts.note: the writer refers to the setter: me
the letters reordered

explanation.surface: A writer makes a nasty dig, and the sting of it could provoke resentment.
explanation.walkthrough: Gall looks like bitterness or cheek, but it is the plant growth: gall midges lay eggs that make plants form galls.
explanation.definitionFit: Gall midges are tiny flies whose larvae cause abnormal swellings, galls, on plant tissue.

clue.text: Master what's extracted from well, getting wet no longer

definitions.note: a verb, 'to wet', marked as obsolete

parts.note: M is an abbreviation for master, as in MA
oil is drawn from an oil well

explanation.surface: A master draws something from a well and dries off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No longer' marks an obsolete sense: moil now means to toil, but once meant to moisten or wet.
explanation.definitionFit: Moil comes from Old French moillier, to moisten, and its original English sense was to make wet.

clue.text: Conclude subject? Not able

indicators.note: 'not' says the following word is to be absent from the longer word

parts.note: subject to, liable to: amenable
taken as written

explanation.surface: A clumsy candidate concludes the topic, being unable to go on.
explanation.definitionFit: To amen something is to say the closing word of a prayer over it, hence to conclude or ratify it.

clue.text: Fair but shunned by company, dejected within, getting rather drunk?

indicators.note: within says one piece is set inside the other
what shuns something keeps away from it, so those letters go

parts.note: fair in looks, comely
Co is the abbreviation for company
low in spirits

explanation.surface: A pretty girl ignored by the crowd gets downcast and drinks too much.
explanation.definitionFit: Mellow means slightly tipsy, and the -y suffix softens it further, so mellowy is somewhat merry with drink.

clue.text: Musician revises aims with these crotchets?

indicators.note: revising reworks something, so its letters are rearranged
the answer is what must join the given word for the rewrite, so it is what is left over once those letters are taken out

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A composer rewrites his goals using quarter notes.
explanation.walkthrough: A composite anagram: the answer plus 'aims' can be rearranged to make 'musician'. Crotchets here are not notes but hooks, the old sense of the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Unci is the plural of uncus, a hook or hooked part; crotchet originally meant a small hook, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Bankrupt making mischief about surplus

indicators.note: about means going around, so one piece surrounds the other

parts.note: impish behaviour is mischief-making
something left over is surplus

explanation.surface: A firm goes bust while someone plays tricks with the leftover money.
explanation.definitionFit: To bankrupt someone, as a verb, is to ruin them financially, which is what impoverish means.

clue.text: Accumulate/fund

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to put resources together in a common stock
second meaning: a shared stock of money

explanation.walkthrough: The slash just separates the verb from the noun.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb the word means combining resources into one store; as a noun it is a common kitty of money.

clue.text: Slalom's beginning at a higher place, bit of work for ski event (6, two words)

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its opening letter

parts.note: only the opening letter is kept
higher up
the erg is a small unit of work in physics

explanation.surface: A slalom racer starts higher up the slope, a bit of effort required for the skiing.
explanation.definitionFit: Super-G, short for super giant slalom, is an Alpine skiing race combining speed with gates.

clue.text: 'Losing weight': lines in lots of printing matter read up

definitions.note: describes something getting smaller; the answer is the comparative adjective

indicators.note: in a down entry, reading upwards means taking the letters from bottom to top
in places one piece inside the other

parts.note: a ream is 500 sheets of paper, and reams means lots
L is the abbreviation for line, doubled for the plural

explanation.surface: A diet article runs to many printed lines, read by someone keen to slim.
explanation.definitionFit: Something losing weight is getting reduced in size, so the comparative 'more little' fits loosely, which the quotation marks hedge.

clue.text: Regular intake to merge with Eton's second

parts.note: die can mean to blend gradually, as one colour dies into another

indicators.note: second points to the letter in position two of the word

parts.note: the word's second letter

explanation.surface: A schoolboy's daily meals get mixed in with the school's second sitting.
explanation.walkthrough: Eton is the English public school. 'Merge' here is die in its fading sense, as in colours dying into one another.
explanation.definitionFit: A diet is the food a person habitually eats, their regular intake of nourishment.

clue.text: Poetry has to be still around in Der Lindenbaum (8, two words)

indicators.note: around means encircling, so one word wraps the other

parts.note: to lie still
poetry is verse, written in metre

explanation.surface: Schubert's song Der Lindenbaum contains poetry that must lie still.
explanation.walkthrough: Der Lindenbaum is a Schubert song from Winterreise; the German title translates straight to the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Lindenbaum is German for the linden, which in Britain is called the lime tree.

clue.text: Old head still taking in all sections

indicators.note: taking something in means admitting it inside

parts.note: still, even now: yet
the as was the Roman whole unit made up of twelve parts, so it is all the sections

explanation.surface: An elderly headmaster is still in charge of every department.
explanation.walkthrough: The reading of 'all sections' as AS is the least certain step: the as was the Roman unit divided into twelve unciae.
explanation.definitionFit: Yeast once also meant froth or foam, the head on a drink, a sense now obsolete.

clue.text: Policeman, for some a bit of a sugar daddy

indicators.note: a bit of a phrase is a run of its letters, taken from inside it

parts.note: the letters run across the two words

explanation.surface: For some people a police officer is something of a generous older benefactor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For some' is fair because the word is Irish: a garda is a member of Ireland's police force, the Garda Síochána.
explanation.definitionFit: The Irish police are the Gardaí, and an individual officer is a garda.

clue.text: Early flight large birds must get about right

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one piece is wrapped round the other

parts.note: geese are large waterfowl
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: Large migrating birds set off early on the correct heading.
explanation.walkthrough: Flight is not birds in the air but a flight of stairs; 'early' marks an obsolete word.
explanation.definitionFit: Greese is an old spelling of grece, a flight of steps or staircase.

clue.text: Fruitcake compounded fat blocking sink

indicators.note: compounded means mixed together, so the letters are blended into a new order
something blocking a channel is stuck inside it

parts.note: to sink, decline or fade away: die
the letters rearranged

explanation.surface: Mixed-up fat from a fruit cake clogs the kitchen sink.
explanation.walkthrough: Fruitcake is slang for a crazy person, not the cake.
explanation.definitionFit: A fruitcake is slang for an eccentric or crazy person, and a daftie is a Scots word for a silly person.

clue.text: Name held by a dignitary pertaining to chain

indicators.note: what is held by something sits inside its grasp

parts.note: taken as written
N is the abbreviation for name
a dean is a church or college dignitary

explanation.surface: A name is kept by a dignitary wearing the chain of office.
explanation.walkthrough: The chain is not a mayor's chain of office but a mountain chain, the Andes.
explanation.definitionFit: Andean means relating to the Andes, the great mountain range of South America.

clue.text: Draw bowl deployed with side

indicators.note: deploying things spreads them out into a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: In cricket, a draw comes when a bowler is used alongside the rest of the side.
explanation.walkthrough: Draw is not a tied match but the verb used of hanging, drawing and quartering: to remove the entrails.
explanation.definitionFit: To draw a carcass is to gut it, and disbowel is an older word for disembowel.

clue.text: Herd on the move split after opening of defile

indicators.note: the opening of a word is its first letter

parts.note: only the first letter is kept
a split or crack is a rift

explanation.surface: Cattle being driven through a narrow pass break up after its entrance.
explanation.definitionFit: A drift is a drove of animals being moved along, especially cattle driven to pasture.

clue.text: Sermonize: 'Some petar (own) will be hoisted'

indicators.note: in a down entry, hoisting lifts the letters so they run upwards
some of a phrase means a portion of its letters, lying inside it

parts.note: the letters run across the two words

explanation.surface: A preacher warns that a man will be hoist with his own petard.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface echoes Hamlet's 'hoist with his own petar', a bomb blowing up its own maker.
explanation.definitionFit: To orate is to speak pompously at length, much like delivering a sermon.

clue.text: Unanswerable question, something that floors you if old

parts.note: a knockout, KO, puts you on the floor
an is an archaic word for if

explanation.surface: A baffling question can knock you flat, if you are elderly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old' belongs to the wordplay: an meaning 'if' is archaic, as in Shakespeare's 'an it please you'.
explanation.definitionFit: A koan is a Zen Buddhist riddle with no logical answer, used to jolt the mind toward insight.

clue.text: King's seal denoting club

parts.note: R stands for rex, Latin for king
an otary is an eared seal, such as a sea lion

explanation.surface: A king's wax seal identifies a private club.
explanation.walkthrough: Seal is the animal, not the stamp: the otary family includes sea lions and fur seals.
explanation.definitionFit: Rotary is the name of the international service club, its members meeting in rotation at one another's premises originally.

clue.text: Kind of arch, I'll be put up over either side of entrance

indicators.note: in a down entry, putting something up turns its letters upwards

parts.note: the ego is the self, the 'I'

indicators.note: a side of a word is one of its end letters, and here both ends are the same

parts.note: either end of the word gives the same letter

explanation.surface: A self-important man promises to be set up above an arched doorway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Over' places the reversed self above the end letter, as a down entry reads.
explanation.definitionFit: An ogee arch has two S-shaped curves meeting at a point, an ogee being an S-shaped moulding.

clue.text: The old tarry tucking into full English

definitions.note: 'the old' marks an obsolete sense of the verb

indicators.note: something tucking into a thing is lodged within it

parts.note: the letters run across the two words

explanation.surface: An old man lingers over his full English breakfast.
explanation.walkthrough: A full English is a British cooked breakfast of eggs, bacon and sausages.
explanation.definitionFit: Leng is an obsolete word for linger or tarry, related to the adjective long.

clue.text: Rickety wicket, say, needing hammer all round (10, two words)

indicators.note: going all round something encloses it completely

parts.note: to malleate is to hammer out metal
e.g. means 'for example', like 'say'

explanation.surface: A rickety cricket wicket needs hammering into shape on every side.
explanation.walkthrough: A wicket is a small gate, not cricket stumps. The mallee is Australian eucalyptus scrub country.
explanation.definitionFit: A mallee gate is Australian for a makeshift gate of wire and posts, a rickety wicket indeed.

clue.text: Trouble and strife directly following from behind

indicators.note: read from behind, the letters run back to front

parts.note: as in due north, directly north
f is the abbreviation for following

explanation.surface: A wife follows on directly, dogging her husband's footsteps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trouble and strife' is Cockney rhyming slang for wife, but here the phrase is meant literally.
explanation.definitionFit: A feud is a long-running bitter quarrel, full of conflict and hostility.

clue.text: Top French army officer Hal dispatched in war

indicators.note: someone dispatched is sent away or killed, so the name goes

parts.note: a Marshal of France is the highest military rank
taken as written

explanation.surface: A senior French general sends Prince Hal off to fight.
explanation.walkthrough: Hal is Shakespeare's young Henry V, which suits a French army surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Mars is the Roman god of war, and his name stands for war itself by metonymy.

clue.text: Cranial eminences visible in brainiacs?

indicators.note: what is visible in a word can be seen inside it

parts.note: the letters sit inside the word

explanation.surface: Clever people show bumps on their skulls.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark nods to phrenology, which read intelligence from bumps on the head.
explanation.definitionFit: Inia is the plural of inion, the bony projection at the back of the skull.

clue.text: Lovely spot, US island — live protected, once battered by storms

definitions.note: 'once' marks the word as old or literary

parts.note: the Vale of Tempe in Greece is proverbial for beauty

indicators.note: what is protected is held safe inside something

parts.note: Staten Island is part of New York City
to live is to be

explanation.surface: A beautiful American island where people once lived sheltered is now lashed by storms.
explanation.definitionFit: Tempest-beaten describes something buffeted by violent storms, a poetic compound.
